docs.title: The Mechanism
docs.text:
The Mechanism (TM) is a research cluster built from found infrastructure: an existing desktop and a disused Raspberry Pi cluster, with a few pieces added where those ran out. It began as an exercise in critical technical practice. The aim was to learn about the affordances and constraints of AI for humanities and social science research by engaging in system design and maintenance myself, not paying for online services where I would be one of many paying customers, or renting cloud infrastructure.

TM is a bespoke system, designed and configured around my own technical and scholarly practices. Its design principles and architecture may be useful more widely, to people designing AI-enabled research platforms, but my focus has been on building a tool for my own research. This site provides high-level documentation intended to convey my motivations and design principles rather than detailed system information.

I am only keeping TM in service because it has proven to be surprisingly useful for my research. It has exceeded my expectations, despite being somewhat fragile beause of its complexity. It is closer to a Heath Robinson machine than a refined computing system, and requires regular (although increasingly manageable) maintenance. I use TM every week, as the primary research tool for my next monograph, Infrastructural Inflections: Critical Technical Practice and the Architecture of Knowledge.

James Smithies, Australian National University. TM is funded by the ANU Futures Scheme (2024–2026), awarded when I joined the ANU.

docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am Professor of Digital Humanities and Director of the HASS Digital Research Hub (HDRH) at the Australian National University. Before ANU I was Professor of Digital Humanities in the Department of Digital Humanities at King's College London. Before then I was founding director of King's Digital Lab and deputy director of King's eResearch. Prior to working at King's I worked as a senior lecturer at the University of Canterbury in Aotearoa/New Zealand, helping develop the UC CEISMIC Canterbury Earthquakes Digital Archive. My doctorate explored the history of ideas in late twentieth-century Aotearoa/New Zealand. I have also worked in the government and commercial IT sectors in the United Kingdom and New Zealand, as a technical writer, editor, business analyst, and project manager.

In my digital practice I apply computational tools and methods to arts, humanities, and social science subjects. This involves the development of products (like websites, electronic books, or mobile applications), the analysis of data (like text, image, and social media archives) and the provision of services (like digital libraries and archives) that can be used to explore subjects as varied as history, literature, philosophy, art history, statistics, and computer science. This sort of work results in traditional scholarly articles and monographs as well as digital outputs. I am interested in any research that involves the innovative application of computational tools and methods to arts, humanities, and social science subjects, and often work in inter-disciplinary teams from across the campus. I have additional experience applying information management techniques to post-disaster contexts.

docs.text:

  • Digital Modernity: Why We Need to Think Historically About the Digital Age. Routledge, 2026. Open access.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: As of October 2026. The Mechanism (TM) is evolving; this page describes its high-level architecture rather than every detail. The full code is kept in a private repository for security purposes.

docs.title: A closed universe
docs.text:
The Mechanism (TM) is designed as a closed universe. The aim was a closed, personal research tool, not an experiment in an open world of agents roaming the internet. I determine what enters the system: my library, the feeds I follow, a handful of structured academic catalogues, and my own messages. Nothing is ingested because an agent decided to search the World Wide Web for it.

That closure is a research choice as much as a security one. It balances the power of agentic AI with a degree of epistemic control and definition that the open internet can't offer. I know and tightly control the epistemic boundaries of the system, ensuring any conceptual work I do with AI agents is defiend on my terms. When an agent answers a question, the boundaries of its Umwelt (world view) are boundaries I set and epxand or reduce as required for my purposes.

Inside that universe, data moves according to a rivers of data model defined by the hardware and network I deisgned and implemented myself. The cluster head is the primary 'headwaters': the point where scheduled work starts, where files are relayed between machines, and through which everything entering or leaving passes. From there data flows down defined channels to the machines and agents that use it, and out to the internet via tightly defined channels such as Zotero or PhilPapers. Each agent is constrained to the data relevant to its function, and reaches nothing else.

docs.title: The stance
docs.text:
TM is a research cluster under one researcher's control, on home hardware. Every external account it uses is a throwaway, created for the purpose, so a compromise means rotating a key and restoring from backup, not a disaster.

What the architecture defends against:

  • A rogue agent. The main concern is an AI agent that reads hostile text, is manipulated by it, and then tries to damage data, reach credentials it shouldn't have, or send data out.
  • Credential leaks from a machine's filesystem.
  • Malformed input that crashes a service.
  • My own mistakes. Through backups and rollback.

What the architecture doesn't try to defend against: a determined state-level adversary deploying social as well as technical techniques, physical access to the machines, compromised upstream software, very slow covert exfiltration, or the compromise of Cloudflare, which sits in front of it.

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Internet
        CF["Cloudflare<br/>tunnel and access control"]
        APIs["Allowed services<br/>(library, model APIs,<br/>academic catalogues)"]
        TG["Telegram"]
        ME["Me, in a browser"]
    end
    subgraph Home["Home network"]
        DT["Desktop<br/>(off the cluster network)"]
        subgraph VLAN["Cluster network (isolated)"]
            HEAD["Cluster head<br/>outbound proxy, relay,<br/>tunnel endpoint"]
            AG["Agent node"]
            JET["Jetson"]
            LIB["Library node"]
            FEED["Feed reader"]
        end
    end
    ME -->|"one-time code"| CF
    CF <-->|"outbound tunnel only"| HEAD
    HEAD -->|"dashboard"| AG
    HEAD -->|"allowlisted requests"| APIs
    AG -->|"polls"| TG
    DT -->|"files only"| HEAD
  • An isolated network. The cluster sits on its own VLAN, separated from the rest of the home network by rules on the router. The desktop, which does the heavy processing, is kept outside it and reaches the cluster only by depositing files.
  • No open ports. Nothing on the cluster accepts connections from the internet. Remote access to the web interfaces runs through azero trust tunnel that the cluster opens outwards, behind a one-time code.
  • Every machine denies by default, in both directions. Inside the cluster network, traffic between machines is governed by each machine's own firewall, which allows only the specific connections that machine needs.
  • One way out. No machine reaches the internet directly. Outbound web requests go through a filtering proxy on the cluster head, and each machine has its own short list of permitted destinations. Anything else is refused and logged. The feed reader is the exception: feeds can come from anywhere, so its requests may go to any destination, but they still pass through the proxy and are logged.

docs.title: Credentials and bridges
docs.text:
Each credential lives on one machine, and the rest of the cluster reaches the service it unlocks through a small bridge that exposes only the operations needed.

Credential Lives on Other nodes get Reference library key Library node A bridge with a fixed set of read and write routes Feed reader key Feed reader A bridge for managing subscriptions and reading entries Model and messaging keys The agent node, in a file only the agent's user can read, and the workflow engine on the cluster head, for the weekly digest and notifications Nothing: no other machine needs them Infrastructure secrets Encrypted in the configuration repository Decrypted only when the configuration is applied

The desktop stores its own library key, for fetching PDFs. It sits off the cluster network, so a compromised cluster machine can't reach it.

docs.title: The agent
docs.text:
The agent is Hermes Agent, an open-source framework from Nous Research, running Claude Opus 5.5 through OpenRouter. I work with it mostly in its browser dashboard and sometimes over Telegram. It is the part of the system most exposed to what it reads, so it gets the least:

  • Its own machine and its own user, with no SSH key. The cluster head refuses SSH connections from it in any case.
  • Four routes into the cluster, each to a narrow service: the read-only corpus API, the library bridge, the feed bridge, and a bridge for writing notes. It can't reach the models or the vector store behind the corpus API.
  • A closed set of inputs. It doesn't fetch arbitrary web pages. What reaches it is my own messages, structured results from a handful of academic catalogues, passages from the corpus, and entries from the feeds I follow. The weekly digest goes a step further: feed items are first scored by a small local model that can return only a structured verdict and has no tools.
  • Operating-system confinement. An AppArmor profile limits what the agent's process can touch.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Model Runs on Used for Qwen3 8B Jetson Triage: scoring feed items for relevance to each research track Qwen3 32B Desktop GPU Describing each passage of every ingested text; triaging new publication records nomic-embed-text Jetson Turning passages and questions into vectors for search Claude Opus 5.5, through OpenRouter Anthropic's cloud The agent: conversation, and answering questions from retrieved passages; primary voice in Workshop sessions Claude Sonnet 5, through OpenRouter Anthropic's cloud Curating the weekly digest from the items Qwen3 8B has scored Gemini 3.8 Flash, through OpenRouter Google's cloud Workshop sessions: devil's advocate, challenging assumptions and finding weaknesses GPT-6 Sol Pro, through OpenRouter OpenAI's cloud Workshop sessions: close reader, focusing on conceptual precision and terminology

docs.title: Software and operations
docs.text:
• Infrastructure as code. Every cluster machine is configured from one repository with Ansible. Services run in Docker containers or as systemd units, and the desktop's jobs run from the same repository under cron.
  • The main components are all open source: Hermes Agent (the agent), Chroma (vector store), Ollama (local models), Syncthing (file transport), n8n (scheduled workflows), Miniflux (feeds), PyMuPDF (text extraction), and Prometheus and Grafana (monitoring). Zotero holds the reference library, and Cloudflare provides the tunnel and access control.
  • Backups run daily to local storage and weekly, encrypted, to cloud object storage. Rollback is treated as a normal operation, not an emergency.
  • Integrity reporting. An hourly check compares what the library says the corpus should contain with what the vector store holds, and reports any drift. A weekly reconciliation also compares the live library's collections directly with the store.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: As of October 2026. The Mechanism (TM) is evolving; this page describes key design decisions rather than every detail. The full code (including all design decisions) is kept in a private repository for security purposes.

docs.title: A weak justification
docs.text:
If I was forced to provide a single justification for TM's continued existence I would point to the balance between the contraption's closed universe of scholarly sources and the power of persistent agentic AI: the balance is difficult to achieve but compelling. My suspicion is that AI-enabled humanities research requires a radical narrowing to high quality sources tailored to the individual researcher, coupled with persistent agentic AI that can guide, critique, and learn alongside the researcher.

This requires a lot more than straight-forward "chat with my pdfs" functionality, but significantly less than access to the entire World Wide Web. TM keeps the researcher firmly at the centre of epistemological and methodological decision-making but with access to the full range of their own sources (primary, secondary, RSS, social media) along with a consistent 'mentor and guide' and a range of configurable 'critical friends'. By keeping as much processing offline as possible and retaining detailed records in offline Markdown files I feel in control. I could continue to work on my monograph project even in the worst case scenario where access to frontier AI is entirely disabled.

Many researchers will also want to choose small and open weight models for some tasks, limiting information leakage to hyperscale AI vendors and reducing the environmental impact of their work as far as possible. Frontier AI services are only accessed intermittently by TM, for advanced text processing and occasional 1-1 discussion sessions and workshops with multiple AI models. Because core TM data only consists of Markdown files and a Zotero library, I could easily migrate my research to another platform if necessary.

This portability and transparency extends to techncial aspects of the project too. I keep a record of architectural decisions in Markdown files in a private code repository, produced as a natural part of my software engineering process but also useful for auto-ethnography in the tradition of Science and Technology Studies (STS). The repository contains extensive documentation alongside Ansible playbooks that document as well as deploy infrastructure as code to TM. More than thirty architectural decisions are stored in the repository. Six examples are listed below.

docs.title: 1. A closed universe of sources
docs.text:
Every external account is a throwaway, and the agent's source inputs are limited to my Zotero library, the RSS feeds I follow, my own messages, and a few structured academic catalogues such as PhilPapers. There is no arbitrary web fetching, and no tool to support it.

Why. An autonomous agent with network access needs a bounded blast radius, especially on a home network, and my research needs to be protected from information leakage and unwanted activity by agents. Throwaway accounts make any compromise a matter of rotating a key and restoring from backup.

The cost. The agent can't discover new sources on its own. That is treated as a feature: every new source, from a book to an article or RSS feed, has to be approved by me. Browser automation is permanently rejected for the same reason. This constraint has turned into one of the system's best affordances. If I need an agent with access to the world I use a standard AI platform.

docs.title: 2. Local models for volume, frontier models for judgement
docs.text:
Work is facilitated by models appropriate to the task. A small model on the Jetson handles high-volume scoring and triage. A larger model on the desktop GPU describes every passage and classifies new publications. Frontier models, reached through an API, provide synthesis and tasks requiring reasoning depth. For structured discussion sessions, the agent convenes one frontier model from each of three families (Anthropic, Google and OpenAI) so the perspectives genuinely differ.

Why. Sending everything to a frontier model would be slow and expensive, and full texts would leave my hardware. On the other hand, running everything locally would sacrifice quality in key areas.

The cost. Two tiers of local hardware to look after (inside and outside the VLAN), and a rule that model versions are pinned exactly. Now that workflow bugs have been ironed out those constraints are not noticeable.

docs.title: 3. One key, one machine
docs.text:
Each credential lives on exactly one machine. Everything else reaches the service through a small bridge that lets it use the service without ever seeing the key.

Why. A compromised agent can search the library, but not copy the key and use it elsewhere.

The cost. More small services to run, and a rule that no new credential-bearing service is deployed until its boundary is defined. In practice I never notice the boundaries between the services; usage is seamless despite the agents being constrained.

docs.title: 4. The closed universe, enforced by the network
docs.text:
Every machine denies outbound traffic by default. The only way out to the web is a filtering proxy on the cluster head, with a separate list of allowed destinations for each machine, and every request it handles is logged. The feed reader is the one exception. Feeds can come from anywhere, so it may request any destination, but only through the proxy.

Why. I have complete control over what sources agents have access to, and what problems they can introduce.

The cost. Each new source needs a deliberate addition. In practice I find I have all the sources I need so this is not an issue.

docs.title: 5. Allowing PDFs to leave the system
docs.text:
The original rule was that copyrighted full texts would never leave my own machines. In practice the Zotero library was already storing every attached PDF on cloud servers, though, and keeping the rule meant filing each book twice: once in the Zotero library, once in a folder on the desktop.

I decided that the Zotero library's cloud storage is a trusted channel. The desktop now fetches PDFs from the library itself. Filing a book in my Zotero library is the only step needed to get it into TM.

What didn't change. Extraction, description and embedding still happen locally. No full text is sent to a cloud model.

Why it's here. It shows what partial sovereignty looks like in practice: considered tradeoffs made on my own judgement and with awareness of the practical impact.

docs.title: 6. Moving triage off the Jetson
docs.text:
Each week the cluster harvests new records from PhilPapers, a large index of philosophy publications, and a model sorts them for relevance to my research tracks. The plan was for the small model on the Jetson to do this. It couldn't: the index returns every record modified that week, often more than 80,000, and at the Jetson's pace one week's file took four days.

Speed wasn't the only problem. The 8-billion-parameter model marked about 0.4% of records as relevant. The 32-billion-parameter model on the desktop marked about 21%. The small model was quietly discarding papers I would have wanted. I relented and moved triage to my desktop computer off TM VLAN.

Why it's relevant. It is the clearest case of finding a performance floor: this was a task the small model could run, but not well enough. By moving up to a more powerful but still local machine, I compromised on system complexity but not data sovereignty.

docs.title: How TM works
docs.text:
As of October 2026. The Mechanism (TM) is evolving; this page provides an overview of some (but not all) of its functionality. The full code is kept in a private repository for security purposes.

The easiest way to understand TM is to explore workflow examples. The two provided below are two of several I use on a regular basis.

docs.title: The machines
docs.text: Machine Role Desktop (GPU workstation) The heavy lifting: fetching PDFs, extracting text, and running Qwen3 32B to describe each passage. Kept off the cluster network by design. Cluster head (Raspberry Pi 5) Coordination: scheduled workflows, monitoring, backups, the web front door, the relay that carries files between machines, and the proxy every outbound request must pass through. Agent node (Raspberry Pi 5) The research agent I talk to: Hermes Agent, an open-source agent framework from Nous Research. It runs on its own machine, as its own user, and holds no keys to the rest of the cluster. Jetson (NVIDIA Orin Nano) The corpus itself: the Chroma vector store, the nomic-embed-text embedding model, Qwen3 8B for triage, all served locally through Ollama, and a read-only API in front of them. Library node (Raspberry Pi 4) The only machine in the cluster holding the reference library's key. It harvests annotations and serves a narrow bridge for library writes. Other Raspberry Pi 4s A feed reader, a social media monitor, and three spares kept powered off.

docs.title: An example workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Z["Reference library<br/>(Zotero)"] -->|"nightly sync"| D["Desktop<br/>fetch, extract,<br/>describe passages"]
    D -->|"files only"| H["Cluster head<br/>relay"]
    H -->|"files only"| J["Jetson<br/>embed and store"]
    Z -->|"hourly"| L["Library node<br/>harvest annotations"]
    L -->|"files only"| H
    J -->|"read-only search"| A["Agent node<br/>Hermes Agent"]
    A <-->|"notes bridge"| O["Obsidian<br/>my notes"]
    O -->|"notes and drafts"| W["Writing<br/>Markdown and Quarto"]
    Z -.->|"references"| W
  1. I file the book or article. In the reference library I add a record with its PDF to the vault collection of a research track. A track is any top-level collection that has a vault child, so the library's own structure is the system's vocabulary. A new track needs no code change.
  2. The desktop fetches it. Every night at 02:00 a sync on the desktop reads the library and fetches new PDFs into a local cache. If the library contradicts itself, for instance when an item has been trashed but its PDF hasn't, the sync refuses to publish that track's changes rather than guess. It reports the problem via Telegram and leaves everything as it was.
  3. The text is extracted and checked. Every six hours the desktop extracts the text. Scanned PDFs with no text layer, and texts too thin to be the whole work (a book yielding fewer than 40 passages, for example), are set aside with a reason, not quietly ingested.
  4. Each passage is described. The text is cut into overlapping passages of about 3,000 characters. For each one, Qwen3 32B, running on the desktop's GPU, writes a one-sentence description of what the passage is about, which makes it much easier to find later. None of this leaves my hardware.
  5. Files travel between machines, commands don't. The results are written as plain files, and Syncthing carries them through the cluster head to the Jetson. The channel moves files only, so nothing on the desktop can instruct anything in the cluster.
  6. The Jetson stores it. Within a minute the Jetson notices the new file, embeds each passage with nomic-embed-text, and stores it in that track's Chroma collection with its bibliographic details.
  7. Annotations follow separately. Every hour the library node harvests my highlights and notes from the library and sends them the same way, into a collection of their own.
  8. The work continues in Obsidian. My primary work with TM is collected in Obsidian notes: plain Markdown files holding lab notes, transcripts of discussion sessions, and drafts. The agent can reach them through a narrow bridge on the cluster head, allowing me to discuss my lab notes, results of previous workshops, and planning and concept development notes for the monograph with Hermes. I can also use Hermes to tidy up or rearrange my notes, or critique my progress and identify errors in my thinking. The Obsidian sync service keeps a copy of all of those notes on my computers, iPad and iPhone.
  9. Writing. I write in Markdown in a separate text editor (and old version of Sublime text), using Quarto (with Zotero) for referencing and footnoting, publishing to .docx or .pdf as required. This is a key step in the process, separating the act of writing from the collaborative human-AI research and concept development undertaken in TM.

docs.title: A question's workflow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    actor Me
    participant C as Cloudflare<br/>tunnel and access check
    participant A as Hermes Agent<br/>agent node
    participant V as Jetson<br/>read-only API
    participant F as Claude<br/>via OpenRouter
    Me->>C: question, in the browser dashboard
    C->>A: through the outbound tunnel
    A->>V: search the corpus
    V-->>A: up to 30 passages, with sources
    A->>F: question and passages, via the outbound proxy
    F-->>A: answer
    A-->>C: answer with citations
    C-->>Me: answer
  1. I ask. Usually in the agent's browser dashboard. Cloudflare checks it's me with a one-time code, then passes the request down a tunnel the cluster itself opened, so nothing on the cluster listens for connections from the internet. I can also message the agent on Telegram, which it polls and which accepts messages only from my account. I use Telegram to interact with Hermes quite frequently when I'm on the go, asking it to write notes to Obsidian or add items to Zotero if necessary.
  2. The agent searches. It sends the question to the Jetson's API. That API is read-only and is the agent's only route to the corpus: it can't reach the store or the models behind it directly.
  3. The Jetson retrieves. It embeds the question with the same model used for the passages, finds the nearest ones, and returns at most 30, each with its source.
  4. A frontier model synthesises. The agent sends the question and those passages, never whole books, to Claude Opus 5.5 through OpenRouter. The request leaves through the cluster head's outbound proxy, which allows the agent only the destinations it needs.
  5. I get an answer with citations via either the Hermes dashboard or Telegram, depending where I asked.

docs.title: What the examples demonstrate
docs.text:
• Local where it matters. Whole texts are fetched, extracted, described, embedded and stored on machines I own. A frontier model only ever sees the few passages a question retrieves.
  • One key, one machine. Each credential lives on the one machine that needs it. The agent, the part most exposed to what it reads, holds the minimum authority to do what it needs to.
  • Narrow channels. Files move one way between the desktop and the cluster in a 'rivers of data' model. The agent reaches the corpus through a read-only API, and every machine reaches the internet only through the proxy.
  • Refusing to guess. When inputs (i.e. scholarly sources) contradict each other, the system stops and alerts me to the discrepancy so I can resolve it myself.
  • Scientific transparency. Zotero remains the canonical storage system for sources and annotations. Outputs from AI sessions are either ephemeral, or captured in lab notes or workshop summaries in Markdown if I ask for them.

docs.title: Engineering and deployment
docs.text: I use VS Code for software engineering, with Claude Code and the OpenSpec framework. The code repository is kept private for security purposes. It contains detailed documentation of the network and security architecture, of necessity given the complexity of the system.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text: Most maintenance is performed in the same way as engineering and deployment, via SSH into the head node and subsequent SSH into nodes with deployment via Ansible, but I have UI access too, via four tools. n8n, Cockpit and Miniflux run on the cluster, behind the same tunnel and one-time code as the agent's dashboard. The Zotero group library is a hosted service.

docs.title: n8n
docs.text:
n8n is the workflow engine on the cluster head. It runs six workflows:

Workflow When What it does Weekly digest Fridays Takes the week's unread feed items, has Qwen3 8B score them, has Claude Sonnet 5 curate the relevant ones, publishes a digest page, and sends me a summary on Telegram. Local backup Daily Backs the cluster up to local storage. Cloud backup Sundays Sends an encrypted backup to cloud object storage. Update check Monthly Compares the pinned versions of deployed services with the latest releases and reports on Telegram. Upgrades are done by hand. Security reminder Quarterly Reminds me on Telegram to run the security review. It checks nothing itself. Save paper On request Checks whether a paper is open access, writes a short summary if it is, files it in a track's queue in the library, and confirms on Telegram.

Telegram delivers digest counts at each stage, so I know when new material is available to review. n8n stores the model and messaging keys and can make outbound requests from the cluster head, so a session there is powerful. It stays behind the one-time code.

docs.title: Cockpit
docs.text:
Cockpit is a web console for Linux servers, installed on every machine in the cluster. It shows each machine's services, logs, and storage in a browser and includes a terminal. Its console provides a UI into each machine, including terminal access.

Cockpit provides root-level administration, so it is treated the same as n8n. Only the cluster head's console is reachable through the tunnel. The others accept connections from the cluster head alone.

docs.title: Miniflux
docs.text:
Miniflux is the feed reader, installed on its own Raspberry Pi 4 with about 90 feeds sorted into 13 categories. Each category maps to a research track, which tells the weekly digest what to judge an item against. Two small helpers sit beside it for sources that don't offer a usable feed: RSSHub, and a proxy for Springer's feeds.

Maintenance here is mostly editorial: adding and removing feeds, and keeping the categories in line with the tracks. The agent can add and remove feeds too, through its bridge, without seeing the key. This allows me to add feeds to TM using Telegram while I'm on the go.

Miniflux entries are marked read only once a run has dealt with them. If a backlog builds up, I mark feeds as read in Miniflux rather than relying on pipeline automation.

docs.title: The Zotero group library
docs.text:
The TM corpus is defined by a Zotero group library called The Mechanism, not by my personal library. My personal library holds about 11,000 items gathered over twenty years and I don't want AI agents to have write access to it. The group library is working material that can be lost if an agent makes a mistake. The agent's bridge is bound to the group library alone, using its own dedicated API key, and the library is private.

The two main tracks in Zotero each have a queue, where saved papers and selections from the RSS digest are placed for manual processing (i.e. for when I have the time to review and/or read and annotate them). Nothing enters the corpus until it is filed into a track's vault collection, so the system relies on me manually filing sources: nothing enters TM without my manual intervention. The other collections are there for my own organisation; the system ignores them except when it is harvesting annotations.

docs.title: Why TM was built this way
The method
docs.text:
The Mechanism (TM) is an exercise in critical technical practice. I could have designed an AI research system on cloud infrastructure, where the machines and the network are out of reach behind someone else's interface, or signed up to a commercial research platform. Instead I built it from what I already had: an existing desktop and a disused Raspberry Pi 4 cluster. Working directly with the physical machines and the network allowed me to explore the possibilities and trade-offs of AI for humanities and social science research first-hand, rather than experimenting with services designed by vendors.

The architecture demonstrates this. It grew around what was available, with several design decisions (especially related to security) emerging by happy coincidence rather than foresight or planning. Three spare nodes sit powered off, for possible future expansion. I resisted incorporating my desktop PC into the system for as long as possible but relented when the small inference board took four days to process one week's batch. Where the found hardware ran out, I added a few pieces: two Raspberry Pi 5s and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano for local inference.

docs.title: A prototype for thinking with
docs.text:
Building TM locally was also a way to understand what AI could do for humanities and social science research at all. When I started, there was no established model for AI enabled research beyond some 'chat to my documents' services. There is still no settled picture of how AI might fit into a full research workflow, from finding and triaging new work, through reading and annotation, to retrieval and writing. Cloud AI services I experimented with felt limited and lacking in an understanding of what humanities research workflows consist of.

A physical prototype made that exploration easier. Each idea could be tried on real machines against a real library, and the result retained, changed, or discarded. The system's scope grow one component and one service at a time, from feed triage to a searchable corpus to an agent working across the whole workflow. Concept development undertaken online, through wireframe diagrams, hosted services, and cloud infrastructure interfaces, would have been less tactile, and I suspect less productive.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
TM is not faster or simpler than using cloud infrastructure or an AI research platform, but efficiency was never the point. Rented infrastructure and digital platforms have a wide range of trade-offs, from limited configuration options, to problems with data soveriegnty, higher monthly costs, and issues with long-term sustainability. Using recycled hardware means I have complete control and can choose to keep it going for as long as the hardware keeps running, upgrading components along the way if they fail or if I need more power.

TM has turned out to be quite cost effective. The project is funded by my ANU Futures Scheme award (2024–2026). The found hardware cost nothing (the Pi cluster was funded by King's College London when I worked there and was sitting in pieces after my migration to Australia), the additional purchases were modest. The cluster only draws about 37 watts, under A$10 a month in electricity. My System 76 Thelio draws significantly more power but is my daily driver PC and only processes TM jobs occassionally. I am currently spending ~A$10 a month for frontier AI tokens. The hardware purchases, the electricity, and an allowance for replacement parts amount to a little over A$40 a month over five years. I plan to run the system for at least that long. I have an upcycled ThinkPad x230 laptop pushing 15 years old: maintaining hardware beyond its shelf-life is a personal hobby. Renting the equivalent (a server for the always-on services plus a GPU on demand for the heavy batches) would cost A$40–80 a month in perpetuity.

It is worth emphasising that TM is not a fully closed system. Synthesis, the processing step where a frontier model is used to read retrieved passages and write abstracts, goes to a commercial model through an API, and the Zotero reference library syncs to Zotero cloud storage. Frontier AI tokens (accessed via Open Router) are used for intensive reasoning and critique when needed. If local models provide enough capability one day I will configure TM as a fully offline system but until then commerical AI is used for burst out capability.
